quote: Warscheinlich nicht. Vielmehr muss eine feste Gerade einmal gegeben sein, sowie ein fester Kreis ausreicht um hernach alles allein durch Lineal zu machen.
english: Probably not. Rather, a fixed straight line must be given once, just as a fixed circle suffices to do everything afterwards with the ruler alone.
topic: Three short notes: Minkowski's conjecture that a closed surface of flexible but inextensible material cannot be continuously bent (especially the sphere); whether all ruler-and-compass constructions can be done with compass alone; and a task to prove that no number in the cyclotomic field other than the root of unity has discriminant equal to the field discriminant.

triage.modern_statement: Compass-only (Mascheroni) constructions: given a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane, can every point constructible with straightedge and compass also be constructed with the compass alone? A line counts as constructed once two of its points are known. Hilbert compared this with the Poncelet–Steiner situation, where a straightedge plus one fixed circle with its center is enough. He guessed the answer was 'probably not' and that a fixed line would have to be given once.
triage.answer_summary_note: Answered YES, so Hilbert's guess was wrong. The result had already been proved before he wrote the note.
triage.answered_by: Georg Mohr, Euclides Danicus (Amsterdam, 1672). This was forgotten and rediscovered in 1928, when J. Hjelmslev republished it in German translation. Lorenzo Mascheroni proved it independently in La geometria del compasso (Pavia, 1797). It is now called the Mohr–Mascheroni theorem. The dual result Hilbert mentions is the Poncelet–Steiner theorem: Poncelet suggested it in 1822 and Steiner proved it in 1833. It says a straightedge alone is enough once one circle and its center are given.

evidence.claim: Mohr–Mascheroni theorem: any construction that can be done with compass and straightedge can be done with a compass alone. Mascheroni discovered it independently in 1797.
Mohr's Euclides danicus (1672) proves that all Euclidean constructions can be done with compasses alone. The book was forgotten until it was found in 1928, and Hjelmslev republished it that year.
Hjelmslev's 1928 republication showed that Mohr had set out Mascheroni's result 125 years before Mascheroni.
Poncelet–Steiner theorem: all Euclidean constructions can be done with a straightedge alone if one circle and its center are given. Poncelet suggested it in 1822 and Steiner proved it in 1833.
There is a contrast with the straightedge-only case: every straightedge-and-compass construction can be done with a compass alone.

triage.why: The question in the note is the classical compass-only construction problem, and it was settled in the affirmative. Mascheroni's 1797 proof was already in print when Hilbert wrote, and Mohr's 1672 proof was rediscovered in 1928. Hilbert's guess that a fixed line would be needed confuses the problem with its dual, the Poncelet–Steiner theorem for the straightedge. That dual result does need extra data (one circle with its center), but the compass-only version needs nothing extra. Variants still appear in the literature, such as discrete versions and versions in non-Euclidean geometries. The core question is closed and is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.
